abstract: Noise is often regarded as anathema to quantum computation, but in some settings it can be an unlikely ally. We consider the problem of learning the class of $n$-bit parity functions by making queries to a quantum example oracle. In the absence of noise, quantum and classical parity learning are easy and almost equally powerful, both information-theoretically and computationally. We show that in the presence of noise this story changes dramatically. Indeed, the classical learning problem is believed to be intractable, while the quantum version remains efficient. Depolarizing the qubits at the oracle’s output at any constant nonzero rate does not increase the computational (or query) complexity of quantum learning more than logarithmically. However, the problem of learning from corresponding classical examples is the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem, for which the best known algorithms have superpolynomial complexity. This creates the possibility of observing a quantum advantage with a few hundred noisy qubits. The presence of noise is essential for creating this quantum-classical separation.

specification.problem: Learn an unknown n-bit parity function f_s(x) = s·x mod 2 (i.e. recover the hidden string s in {0,1}^n) from a quantum example oracle whose n+1 output qubits are each subjected to depolarizing noise at a constant rate p, using a number of oracle queries and computation that grows at most logarithmically beyond the noiseless case, in contrast to the classical Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem.
specification.reconstruction_scope: One smallest useful construction: the Bernstein–Vazirani-style Hadamard-transform learner applied to noisy quantum examples, for a tiny explicit instance n = 3, hidden string s = (1,0,1), single-qubit depolarizing rate p = 0.1 applied independently to all n+1 oracle output qubits, with m repeated queries and a per-bit correlation estimate as classical postprocessing. Outside scope: the paper's precise noise model and algorithm (only inferred here), the formal proof that noise costs only a logarithmic factor, the classical LPN hardness comparison, the 'few hundred qubits' resource estimate, and the claim that noise is essential for the separation.

symbols.meaning: Number of input bits of the parity function; also number of data qubits
Hidden parity string defining the target concept
Input string to the parity function / computational basis label of the data register
Parity of x on the support of s
Depolarizing rate applied to each oracle output qubit
Latent branch bit of a single measured sample (which GHZ-like branch is observed)
Effective bit-flip noise on measured qubit i
Measured outcome: y on the n data qubits, b on the label qubit
Target failure probability of the learner

equations.label: Parity concept class
equations.latex: f_s(x) = s \cdot x \bmod 2 = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} s_i x_i, \qquad s, x \in \{0,1\}^n
equations.description: Definition of the n-bit parity function labelled by the hidden string s; the learning task is to recover s exactly.
equations.abstract_quote: learning the class of $n$-bit parity functions
equations.justification: The abstract names the concept class; the standard definition of a parity function is the inner product mod 2 with a hidden string.
assumptions: Standard definition of parity functions; no affine offset is included.

equations.label: Noiseless quantum example oracle state
equations.description: Each oracle query returns the uniform superposition of labelled examples; register D (qubits 1..n, qubit i holds x_i) carries the input and register L (qubit n+1) the label.
equations.justification: The Bshouty–Jackson quantum example oracle under the uniform distribution is the standard meaning of 'quantum example oracle'; the abstract does not write the state explicitly.
assumptions: Examples are drawn from the uniform distribution over inputs.
Register ordering: data qubits 1..n then label qubit n+1.

equations.label: Single-qubit depolarizing noise on oracle output
equations.description: Every one of the n+1 output qubits is depolarized independently at constant rate p before the learner acts.
equations.justification: Textbook depolarizing channel; the abstract says the output qubits are depolarized at a constant rate but does not specify whether noise is per-qubit i.i.d., so the product form is a modelling choice.
assumptions: Independent, identical depolarizing noise on each output qubit with the same rate p.
Noise acts only at the oracle output; the learner's gates and measurements are noiseless.

equations.label: Hadamard transform of the noiseless example state (exact)
equations.description: The Bernstein–Vazirani identity: a Hadamard on all qubits maps the example state to an equal superposition of the all-zero branch and the branch revealing s with label 1. This equality is exact.
equations.justification: Standard Fourier-sampling computation: sum over x of (-1)^{y·x + b(s·x)} vanishes unless y = b s.

equations.label: Computational-basis outcome distribution of one noisy sample
equations.latex: \Pr[(y,b)] = \sum_{c \in \{0,1\}} \frac{1}{2} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^{[y_i \neq c s_i]} \left(1-\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^{[y_i = c s_i]} \left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^{[b \neq c]} \left(1-\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^{[b = c]}
equations.description: Equivalently y_i = c s_i ⊕ e_i and b = c ⊕ e_{n+1} with c uniform and e_i i.i.d. Bernoulli(p/2). Uses that Λ_p commutes with H and acts as a bit-flip with probability p/2 on computational-basis statistics; off-diagonal (coherence) terms do not affect this distribution.
equations.justification: Derived by combining eq_3 and eq_4 for the chosen construction; the actual paper's measurement procedure is not given in the abstract.
assumptions: Learner applies H^{⊗(n+1)} then measures all n+1 qubits in the computational basis.

equations.label: Per-bit correlation statistic distinguishing s_i
equations.description: For s_i = 1, y_i and b agree iff the two noise bits agree; for s_i = 0, y_i is pure noise and b carries the uniform branch bit, so agreement is exactly 1/2. The gap 1/2 - p + p^2/2 is a positive constant for any constant p < 1.
equations.justification: Direct consequence of eq_5; chosen as a simple classical estimator consistent with the abstract's claim that constant-rate noise costs only a logarithmic factor.
assumptions: Estimator choice is the reconstructor's; the paper may use a different postprocessing rule.

equations.label: Query complexity under noise (asymptotic, not exact)
equations.description: By a Hoeffding bound on the empirical agreement frequency for each bit and a union bound over n bits, m noisy queries suffice; for constant p this is O(log n) versus O(1) queries in the noiseless case, i.e. at most a logarithmic increase.
equations.abstract_quote: Depolarizing the qubits at the oracle’s output at any constant nonzero rate does not increase the computational (or query) complexity of quantum learning more than logarithmically.
equations.justification: The abstract asserts the logarithmic overhead; the specific bound follows from eq_6 via standard concentration inequalities for the assumed estimator.
assumptions: Big-O hides constants; this is an upper bound, not an exact count.

registers.name: D (data)
registers.role: Holds the example input x; qubit i encodes x_i. After Hadamard, reveals s on the b=1 branch.

registers.name: L (label)
registers.role: Holds the parity label f_s(x); after Hadamard indicates which branch (all-zero or s) was observed.

specification.initial_state: Per query, the oracle supplies ρ_out = Λ_p^{⊗(n+1)}(|ψ_s⟩⟨ψ_s|) on registers D⊗L (eq_2, eq_3); the learner holds no additional qubits. Instance: n = 3, s = (1,0,1), p = 0.1.

steps.description: Query the noisy quantum example oracle once to obtain ρ_out on the n+1 qubits D⊗L.
Apply H to every qubit of D and L (noise commutes with H, so the state is Λ_p^{⊗(n+1)} applied to the GHZ-like state of eq_4).
Measure all n+1 qubits in the computational basis, obtaining (y,b) distributed as in eq_5.
Repeat the query–Hadamard–measure cycle m times, collecting samples (y^{(k)}, b^{(k)}), k = 1..m.
Classically estimate each s_i from the agreement frequency between y_i^{(k)} and b^{(k)}, thresholding at the midpoint of the two values in eq_6.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of all n+1 qubits after the Hadamard layer on each of the m queries; outcome (y,b) ∈ {0,1}^n × {0,1} per query.
specification.classical_postprocessing: For each i, compute a_i = (1/m) Σ_k [y_i^{(k)} = b^{(k)}]; set ŝ_i = 1 if a_i > (1/2 + 1 - p + p²/2)/2 = 3/4 - p/2 + p²/4, else ŝ_i = 0. Optionally verify ŝ against a few fresh samples. For the instance p = 0.1 the two agreement probabilities are 0.905 (s_i = 1) and 0.5 (s_i = 0).
assumptions: No experiment_scope was provided; the n = 3, s = (1,0,1), p = 0.1 instance and the Hadamard-plus-correlation learner are the reconstructor's choice of smallest useful construction.
The quantum example oracle is the Bshouty–Jackson uniform-distribution oracle.
Depolarizing noise is i.i.d. per output qubit at rate p and the learner's own operations are noiseless.
The per-bit agreement estimator (eq_6) is a plausible, not sourced, realization of the paper's efficient noisy learner.
missing_information: The paper's exact noise model (whether depolarizing is per-qubit i.i.d., the rate parameterization, and whether the label qubit is treated differently).
The paper's actual algorithm and proof giving the logarithmic overhead, including explicit constants in the query and computational complexity.
Details of the classical LPN comparison and the quantitative resource estimate behind 'a few hundred noisy qubits'.
The argument that noise is essential for the quantum–classical separation.
